turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was something near the bottom of the screen, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "there was something near the bottom of the screen, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large dark "Continue Shopping" button positioned near the bottom of the screen, sitting prominently above the "Place Order" element — its label and placement felt unexpected for a checkout layout.

B) The "Place Order" button at the very bottom of the screen, which appears visually muted and lower in weight compared to the "Continue Shopping" button directly above it.

C) The small-print legal text block at the very bottom of the screen, positioned beneath both action elements, whose purpose or relationship to the rest of the layout was unclear.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably B? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: What kind of task were you trying to get done when you were looking at this screen?
turns.a: I suppose just... complete the transaction. Get it submitted. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like a step in something larger. Someone else usually handles the follow-up.

turns.q: When you noticed the "Place Order" button sitting lower in the visual hierarchy than "Continue Shopping," what were you trying to confirm about how the screen was organized?
turns.a: "Get the order in correctly on the first attempt. That's the key part — not just submit it, but make sure the information is right and that it actually goes through. When you're doing this for a group, having to redo it is more than just your own time."

turns.q: If the visual weight and placement of "Place Order" were adjusted in this layout, what would tell you the screen had successfully communicated which action matters most?
turns.a: "A confirmation page or message that's immediately visible — an order number or reference. Under 60 seconds from submitting to having something confirmed. No second-guessing, no having to reload or go back to check. That's the success state."

turns.q: When you look at the "Place Order" button on this screen, what is it about its appearance — the fill, the color, or the border — that makes it read as lower priority than the button above it?
turns.a: I mean... it was just a small thing. The button wasn't as prominent as I expected. Most of the time I'd figure it out. It's not a blocker, exactly.

turns.q: Looking at just the "Place Order" button itself — does it have a solid colored fill, or does it appear hollow, outline-only, or closer to plain text?
turns.a: The problem is visibility, really. The button to submit — the 'Place Order' button — didn't look like a primary action. It looked like a label. So I spent time looking for something that was already there, just... not visible enough.

turns.q: Between the "Place Order" button and the "Continue Shopping" button above it — which one has a solid colored fill, and which one looks more like an outline or plain text?
turns.a: The button was gray on a gray background with very small text — 12 pixels, I think. For the primary action on the screen, that's basically invisible. I couldn't tell if it was meant to be interactive, if it was disabled, or if I was just overlooking it. The barrier is the contrast. To remove it: give the 'Place Order' button a solid fill color that actually stands out from the background, and increase the text to something legible — 16 pixels minimum. That's the change. Everything else on the screen was fine.

missed_unlock_opportunities: The interviewer reached near-unlock proximity by turns 3–6 but did not secure a confirmed concrete step in the chain, missing chances to pin down the exact task, success condition, or visual cue tied to the bottom-screen action.

After the participant signaled hesitation around the Place Order control, the interviewer could have asked for the single cue that made it feel non-actionable and confirmed it as a barrier before moving on.

When the discussion approached the desired confirmation state, the interviewer missed an opportunity to redirect back to what the participant saw in the moment and what specifically prevented confident submission.
